full_judgment:
3. The suit was contested by Defendants Nos. 1 to 5 as well as by Defendant Nos. 27 to 48 and 50 to 61 who filed two separate written statements. Defendant Nos. 1 to 5 pleaded inter alia that the suit was not maintainable in the present form and was bad for defect of parties and misjoinder of parties and causes of action and alleged that the genealogy and the sequence of death as given in the plaint were incorrect and that the suit was barred by limitation and adverse possession. The main contention of the said Defendants as stated in their written statement was however that it was true that the suit properties did originally belong to Rajab Ali and that Rajab Ali died leaving behind not only two sons and a widow but also 6 daughters who inherited the suit property but that they being satisfied with the conduct of Defendant Nos. 1 to 5 and dissatisfied with the rude behavior and unkind treatment of Aziz Baksh, relinquished and gave up their -/8/8 gondas share of the disputed land in favour of Jalal Baksh and got the same recorded in the name of Jalal Baksh along with his own share to the knowledge of Aziz Baksh who raised no objection. Thereafter by amicable partition of the suit land by metes and bounds with his brother Aziz Baksh, Jalal Baksh possessed his -/11/4 gondas share of the suit land duly demarcated till his death. After the death of Surati Bibi the share of Jalal Baksh increased to /12/4 gondas share which was also duly demarcated. It is therefore alleged that the suit lands having already been partitioned amicably, there was no scope for further partition. 

 5. Several issues were framed and the learned Subordinate Judge on a consideration of the evidence on record has come to the finding that the suit is not bad for mis-joinder of parties or causes of action nor for defect of parties and that the suit is maintainable in its present form. The learned Subordinate Judge has further held that the case made out in the plaint that Rajab Ali died leaving only two sons and a widow and no daughter is not correct and that he was survived by the 6 (six) daughters as contended by the contesting defendant Nos. 1 to 5 . On the question of the alleged gift and relinquishment of the shares of the sisters in favour of their brother Jalal Baksh, the learned Subordinate Judge has come to a definite finding on a consideration of the evidence on record and the circumstances of the case that 6 daughters of Rajab Ali did not gift away, relinquish or give up their shares of the suit land to Jalal Baksh and get the some recorded in the name of Jalal Baksh in the C.S. record. It has been further held on the basis of the said finding that the entries in the C.S. records of right regarding -/11/4 gondas share in the name of Jalal Baksh are wrong and have no basis whatsoever. On the question of the alleged amicable partition the learned Subordinate Judge has held on a consideration of the evidences on record that the suit lands were never mentioned by metes and bounds between Jalal Baksh and Aziz Baksh. With regard to the registered deed Ext. A evidencing an amicable partition as amongst the plaintiffs Nos. 1 to 4 the learned Subordinate Judge has held that the said document is not a legally valid one as other co-sharers were not parties to the same. The properties sought to be partitioned by the said document, according to the learned Subordinate Judge, are still joint and liable to be partitioned. On the question or the bar of limitation and adverse possession as has been pleaded by the contesting Defendant No. 1 to 5 the learned Subordinate Judge has come to the finding that 6 sisters of Jalal Baksh and Aziz Baksh used to possess the suit land constructively through their brothers by enjoying the usufructs of the joint lands or coming to their paternal house from time to time and therefore the question of limitation or of adverse possession does not at all arise in the present case. 

 11. Mr. Jani Alam, the learned Advocate for the appellants has next contended that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in not holding that the contesting Defendants Nos. 1 to 5 had acquired valid tine with regard to -/11/- annas 4 gondas share by adverse possession. The learned Advocate has submitted that the record of right showing that Jilal Baksh was in possession of -/11/4 gondas share was a clear evidence of his assertion of hostile title and that the continuous exclusive possession of Jalal Baksh and his heirs in accordance with the entries in the records of right and non-participation in the rents and profits of the lands by the sisters of Jalal Baksh and or their heirs provides a sufficient basis for holding that the Jalal Baksh and his heirs have been exercising acts of possession in the major share of the properties to the exclusion of the other co-sharers in respect of the said share. 

 13. It has however been contended before us that it has been held in some cases that there is another proposition of law recognized by the judicial authorities to the effect that non-participation in the rents and profits of a certain property by a co-owner for a considerable length of time may give rise to a presumption of ouster. Relying upon this principle the leaned Advocate for the appellants has submitted that exclusive possession of the joint lands by Jalal Baksh and his heirs to the extent of 11 annas 4 gondas share for more than the statutory period has, in their circumstances of the case, resulted in the extinguishment of the interests of the sisters of Jalal Baksh in the joint lands and acquisition of the said interests by him. 

 17A. Sir Lawrence Jenkins, as the Chief Justice of the Bombay High Court had to deal with a similar question in a Second Appeal in the case of Gangadhar Vs. Paraihram (1905) I.L.R. 29 Bom. 340 and following the above mentioned case refused to interfere with a finding of ouster on the basis of the evidence of exclusive possession of a tenant-in-common for nearly 40 years, as it was impossible, according to the learned Chief Justice to say that there was no evidence in support of the said finding. As this decision has sometimes been cited in support of the proposition that mere non-participation in the rents and profits of a joint property for a long period may lead to a presumption of ouster the statement of law made by Mr. Justice Ashhurst in the case of Fisher and Taylor Vs. Prosser (1774) 1 Cowper 217 on which reliance was placed by the learned Chief Justice may be quoted as follows: 

 21A. It may be noticed that in Varada Pillal's case it had not been necessary to apply the above quoted dictum as the person claiming adverse possession against her co-sharers had no interest in the land at the time when she was put into possession of the same by the two co-owners who wanted to invest full rights upon her and the possession which had been adverse against the said co-owners since the commencement of her possession did not cease to be so when on a subsequent date she inherited a moisty of the said land on the death of one of the said two co-owners. Nonetheless, the said dictum has sometimes been referred to in support of the proposition that mere non-participation in the rent and profits of a joint property for a long period is sufficient to lead to an inference of ouster. It is however pertinent to note what the court was considering in the Colley's case was the question of adverse possession against a tenant in common in an action of ejectment and it was pointed out there that in order to find ouster, in addition to non-participation other circumstances much concur and the matter was to be left to the jury to decide whether in the circumstances of the case, ouster could be presumed. This other circumstances points to the circumstances in which it is not possible to hold that the possession of one co-tenant is the possession of the other as has been stated in the first part of the passage, and is obviously referable to the state of mind of the person in exclusive possession as well as of the person against whom the adverse claim is sought to be made. The person in possession is to abandon his character of a co-sharer and this he cannot do, as was pointed out by the Judicial Committee in the case of Corea Vs. Appnhamy, by a secret intention in his mind. He can be shorn of his character which law attributes to him only if he gives notice of the change of his intention to the person most affected by it viz. his co-sharer on whose behalf he had been possessing all this time. 

 22. The Calcutta High Court has considered this question as to non-participation in the rents and profits of a joint property for a long time being the evidence of ouster in a number of cases, and the preponderant view expressed in the said cases some of which have been mentioned below following the various decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council referred to above, is that mere non-participation in the rents add profits of a joint property by a co-sharer for a long period would not be sufficient to give rise to the inference of ouster and that there is ouster only when there is an assertion of a hostile title by one co-sharer against the others to the knowledge of the lattet : Lokenath Singh Vs. Dhakeswar Prasad, 20 C.W.N. 51 same case 21 C.L.J. 253; Balaram Garin Vs. Shyama Charon, 24 C.W.N. 1057 same case 33 C.L.J. 344, Jagahnath Marwari Vs. Sm. Candni Bibi, 26 C.W.N. 65 same case 34 C.L.J. 432, Joy Narayan Sen Ukil Vs. Sri-kantha Roy, 26 C.W.N. 206 same case 33 C.L.J. 592: Jogendra Nath Vs. Rajendra Nath, 26 C.W.N. 890 same case A.I.R. 1922 Cal. 54, Moulavi Abdul Wahed Vs. Mohon Bashi Saha, 34 C.W.N. 246 same case A.I.R. 1930 Cal. 466; Jagidlsh Vs. Tayab Sardar, I.L.R. 61 Cal. 377 same case A.I.R. 1934 Cal. 644 and Nerasal Chandra Vs. Mohltosh 40 C.W.N. 777 same case A.I.R. 1936 Cal. 466 

 "The fundamental rule is that in order to establish adverse possession as between co-sharers, there must be evidence of an open assertion of hostile title by one of them to the knowledge of the others; mere non-participation in the profits by one party and exclusive occupation by the other is not conclusive." 

 23B. In the case of Nirinal Chandra Vs. Monitosh, reliance was placed on behalf of one of the contending parties upon the passage from the judgment in Calley Vs. Deo d. Taylorson, as Us already been quoted at pages 26-27 of this judgment in support of the proposition that mere non-participation in the rents and profits by a co-sharer for a long period would constitute ouster and D. N. Mitter, J, in delivering the judgment in the said case made the following comment at page 787 of 40 C.W.N. 

 "This case does not support the broad proposition formulated that dispossession or non-possession for a considerable length of time is sufficient to give rise to an inference of ouster. The words which have been italicised, namely 'other circumstances concur are of very great materiality. It is a some-what dangerous doctrine to profound that mere non-participation of rents and profits of joint property by a co-sharer for a very long period would be sufficient to give rise to the inference of ouster". 

 23C. It seems to us that there had been a consensus of judicial opinion, so far as the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and the Calcutta High Court were concerned, as to the law of adverse possession against a co-sharer and knowledge of the non-possessing co-sharer as to the hostile intent of the co-sharer in possession was considered to be an essential element for establishing such possession to be adverse. 

 "Now, the ordinary classical requirement of adverse possession is that it should be nec vi nec clam nec precario (see. Secretary of State for India Vs. Debendralal Khan, 61 I.A. 78 same case A.I.R. 1934 P.C.23. The possession required must be adequate in continuity, in publicity and in extent to i show that it is possession adverse to the competitio (See Radhanoni Debi Vs. Collector of Khulna, 27 I.A. 136) But it is well settled that in order to establish adverse possession of one co-heir as against another it is not enough to show that one out of them is in sole possession and enjoyment of profits, of the properties. Ouster of the non-possessing co-heir by the co-heir in possession who claims possession to be adverse should be made out. The possession of one co-heir is considered in law, as possession of all the co-heirs. When one co-heir is found to be in possession of the properties it is presumed to be on the basis of joint title. The co-heir in possession cannot render his possession adverse to the other co-heir not in possession by an secret hostile animus on his own part in derogation of the other co-heir's title (see Corea Vs. Appuhamy (1912) A.C. 230). It is a settled rule of law that as between co-heirs there must be evidence of open assertion of hostile title, coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment by one of them to the knowledge of the other so as to constitute ouster. This does not necessarily mean that there must be an express demand by one and denial by the other." 

 24B. The learned Judge of the Indian Supreme Court, it will appear from the above-quoted passage, had no hesitation in pointing out that it was a settled rule of law that knowledge of the excluded co-sharer as to the adverse claim of the possessing co-sharer was an essential element of ouster, but he proceeded further to observe in the said case that there were cases in which it had been held that ouster could be inferred from "notorious exclusive possession" of a co-sharer" in assertion of hostile title" for a very considerable time and the excluded co-sharer did not take any step to vindicate his title and added that it was not necessary to decide whether that line of cases were right or wrong. It should, however, be noticed that the learned Judge was not referring while making the above-mentioned observation, to those cases which endorsed the view that mere exclusive possession by a co-owner for a very long periods and nothing more was sufficient to give rise to an inference of ouster. The line of case about the correctness of which the Indian Supreme Court appears to have refrained from expressing any definite view in the aforementioned case, were obviously, those in which there was exclusive possession in open assertion of hostile title and it was notorious for a considerable length of time. In these cases, it has been held that although there was no express notice the non-possessing co-sharer was presumed to have derived his knowledge from the notorious acts of the possessing co-sharer, which were done in open assertion of hostile title for a considerable length of time. In our opinion, the line of difference between these two classes of cases is very thin. In one class of cases there is positive evidence of the knowledge of the non-possessing co-sharer, but in the other class, the knowledge is inferred from certain circumstances. 

 29A. In support of this proposition, several decisions of the Calcutta High Court, two decisions of the Bombay High Court and one decision of the Judicial Committee, most of which been considered by us earlier, have been mentioned. Although Mr. Justice Guha has made the above statement as if it were a different principle independent of the general principle of ouster of a co-sharer, and has included in the list of the decisions mentioned above the two judgments of Sir Lawrence Jenkins pronounced in the Gangadhas case (29 Bom. 300) and Ayennessa Bibi's case (16 C.W.N. 849), the judgment of Nasim Ali J in Krishna Chandra's case (60 C.L.J. 232) and that in Chand Bhai's ease (46 Bom. 213) which are sometimes cited in support of the extreme proposition that mere non-participation in the rents and prate of a joint property by a co-owner may give rise to an inference of ouster against him, the learned Judge has not, in our opinion, added the authority of the Court for such a proposition in the said passage. This is obvious from the fact that the learned Judge has included in the said list not only the Privy Council case of Varada Pillar but also the two cases of the Calcutta High Court, viz. Balaram Guria Vs. Shyama Charan, 24 C.W.N. 1059 and Nirmal Chandra Vs. Mohintosh, 40 C.W.N. 777 in which it was pointed out that more non-participation in the rents and profits by a co-owner could not be the foundation of a finding of ouster. Mr. Justice Mitter has expressed him-self rather strongly in Nirmal Chandra's case, by deprecating the proposition as a dangerous doctrine. It should also be noticed that the decision on the question of ouster of the co-sharers was rested in the said case of the Dacca High Court on a definite finding of their knowledge of the adverse claim. 

 30B. On a critical examination of the various judicial authorities on the question of this important branch of the law of limitation, we thus find that it is well settled that the knowledge of the non-possessing co-sharer as to the adverse claim of the possessing co-sharer is an essential element in making the latter's possession adverse against the former. We have noticed the distinguished views of the Judicial Committee and other learned Judges in this regard. An analysis of the relevant provisions of the Limitation Act also lead us to the same conclusion. Under section 28 of the Limitation Act a person's right to a property is extinguished at the determination of the period limited to him by the Limitation Act for instituting a suit for possession of the said property and under Art. 144 of the Schedule to the Act, the period of limitation is 12 years for instituting such suit and the said period of limitation starts running from the way "when the possession of the defendant becomes adverse, to the plaintiff". When a person without a claim of title gets into possession ousting a rightful person, there is no difficulty to determine the point of time when such possession becomes adverse to the latter, because possession is adverse from the very inception. But it is not so in the case of a co-sharer in exclusive possession of a joint property, because such possession is consistent with joint title and it becomes adverse only when the possessing co-sharer denies the title or right of the non-possessing co-sharer and a right to sue accrues to such non-possessing co-sharer. As has been pointed out in Corea's case, this cannot happen by a secret change of mind. The non-possessing co-sharer must know that there has been a change in animus and a right to sue the possessing co-sharer for recovery of possession has accrued to him. It appears to be an absurd proposition to contend that it does not matter whether the non-possessing co-sharer knows of the hostile intent of the possessing co-sharer or not a right to sue accrues to him and time starts running against him as soon as the possessing co-sharer conceives a malafide intention against his co-sharer within his mind or express it to some-body else. Without his knowledge with the result that the co-sharer out of possession ultimately loss his property without ever being given a chance to redeem the same. This view of law is certainly not in keeping with the principle of justice and good 'conscience and in an opinion the Legislative could not have enacted the said provision of the Limitation Act by attributing to it a meaning which has the effect of depriving a co-owner of his property without any conceivable lapse on his part. He should have been given an opportunity to know that rightful possession of his co-owner has become unlawful. As has been pointed out in the cases referred to above, the person concerned need not be notified or informed by an express notice, but it is sufficient if the circumstances show that such knowledge may be reasonably inferred. 

 32. Mr. Jani Alam, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants has next contended that having regard to the admitted position that a certain plot was said by Aziz Baksh to one Gadu and the said plot has again been transferred to one Asak Mondal who has been examined as D.W. 5 in this case, the Trial Court ought to have held that the suit being a partition suit was not maintainable in the absence of the said transferee. The learned Advocate has also submitted that admittedly one Abdur Rashid who happens to be a son of Defendant No. 25 is also a transferee of a part of the suit land from the plaintiff and the plaintiffs respondent took out a Rule in this Court being C.R. No. 1872 (f) of 1969 praying for a remand of the suit to the Trial Court to enable the plaintiffs to have a retrial of the suit after adding Abdur Rashid a party to the suit. The said rule, of course, has been discharged for non-prosecution as the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners of the said Rule has submitted that he had instruction not to press the said Rule. The learned Advocate for the appellant has contended that the said Abdur Rashid being admittedly a co-sharer in respect of certain plots in the suit, the suit is clearly not maintainable because of non-joinder of the said Abdur Rashid. 

 33. It may be pointed out that in the written statement no objection as to the defect of parties on the ground of non-impleading Asak Mondal or Abdur Rashid was taken. Although the general ground of defect of party was taken, the plaintiffs served a notice upon Defendant Nos. 1 to 5 with interrogatories for supplying the names of the persons who according to them were interested in the suit properties and should be impleaded. In answer to the said interrogatories Defendant Nos. 1 to 5 supplied certain names who according to them were interested in the properties in suit and therefore should be impleaded. After receiving the said names the plaintiffs added all those persons as patties defendants to this suit. But in the list given by the defendants the name of Asak or Abdur Rashid was not included. At the time of the hearing, however, evidence was led to the effect that there was a transfer of certain plot by Aziz Baksh to a certain person who again has sold it to Asak Mondal, although no registered deed has been put into evidence in support of the alleged transfer to Asak Mondal. It is not known whether he is in possession of any part of the disputed property on the strength of the said deed of transfer. As regards the transfer in favour of Abdur Rashid, it is the case of the plaintiff-respondents in their application in the Civil Rule referred to above that the said Abdur Rashid lives in joint mess with his father Defendant No. 25 and that on the idea that Defendant No. 25 is the real owner. Abdur Rashid was not impleaded as a party defendant. 

 35. On the question of non-joinder of parties reference may be made to the provisions of Order 1 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil procedure in which it has been laid down that no objection on the ground of non-joinder of parties shall be given effect to unless it has been taken at the earliest possible opportunity and when such objection has not been so taken, it shall be deemed to have been waived. It is clear therefore that in view of the said provision the appellants are not entitled to raise the question of non-joinder of Asak or Abdur Rashid for the first time At the hearing of the suit when they have not taken such a plea at the earliest opportunity and have not included their napes in the list of the necessary parties supplied by theta while submitting answers to the interrogatories served upon them at the instance of the plaintiffs. 

 36. This question, however, is subject to another legal principle. It is not doubt true that the party to a suit shall not be allowed to agitate the question of non-joinder or mis-joinder of parties at a subsequent stage if such a plea has not been taken at the earliest opportunity. But there is also another principle which has received judicial recognition, according to which no court shall pass an infructuous decree. If it is found on a consideration of the evidence on record that a necessary party has not been impleaded in consequence whereof the decree which may be passed in the suit may be set at naught at the instance of the non-impleaded person, such a decree shall not be passed by a Court. This question was considered in a decision given by a Division Bench of this Court to which one of us is a party in the case of Asadunnessa and others Vs. Qumarazzaman and others, reported in 26 DLR (Dac.) at 363 in which the above mentioned principle of law, has been recognized. 

 37. In the present case, we are therefore to see whether there are sufficient materials on record from which we can say that a necessary party has really not been impleaded in the suit and that as such the decree which has been passed shalt be rendered in fructuous at the instance of such non-impleaded person. We have already noted that proper evidence in this regard has not been adduced in this case. None of the deeds of transfer on the basis of which the said non-impleaded persons namely Asak Mondal and Abdur Rashid have been produced it Court. In our opinion, oral evidence in support of a transfer which is made by a registered document is not proper evidence for proving the said act of transfer. In the absence of such a document it is difficult for us to hold that the said persons have acquired valid title to the disputed property in suit or any part thereof. Moreover, we are of the opinion that in any view of the matter the decree which has been passed in this partition suit cannot be rendered infructuous even if the said persons have some interest in any portion of the property in suit. According to the evidence which has been sought to be adduced in this respect the said persons have acquired, if at all, interest in some specific plots of the suit properties. The alleged transferees have not claimed any interest in the whole of the properties in the suit and as such they have no community of interest in the entire suit properties along with the others having interest therein. In the said circumstances it can at most be contended that any defect which may have crept in the frame of the suit because of not-empleading the said two persons having interest in the aforesaid two plots, the final decree which may be passed in this suit may be infructuous with regard to the said two plots only in which the said persons claim Some interest, but the rest of the decree will remain unaffected. Furthermore the said transferees may remain satisfied with the allotments which may be allocated to their predecessors in interest. 

 40. In the present case, we think it is up to the said persons, if they are so advised, to press their claim with regard to their property at the time of the preparation of the final decree in the Trial Court. In view of the facts of the case, we are of the opinion that the decree need not be set aside on the ground of non-impleading the aforesaid Asak and Abdur Rashid. We, therefore, do not find any substance in any of the contention raised by the learned Advocate for the appellants.
